parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
A long straight vertical wire A carries a current in an upward direction. The wire passes through the centre of a horizontal card, as illustrated in Fig. 10.1.
{{figure:figure_10_1}}
Fig. 10.1
The card is viewed from above. The card is shown from above in Fig. 10.2.
{{figure:figure_10_2}}
Fig. 10.2
On Fig. 10.2, draw four lines to represent the magnetic field produced by the current-carrying wire.

markscheme_points.text: concentric circles centred on the wire
separation of lines increasing with distance

hints: Hint 1: Imagine looking straight down along the wire in Fig. 10.2 with current coming out toward you. What symmetrical shape must the field lines have in the plane of the card?
Hint 2: Think about how the strength of the field changes as you move further from the wire, and what that means for how closely the field lines should be drawn together.
Hint 3: Use your right hand with thumb pointing out of the page along the current. Which way do your fingers curl when viewed from above, clockwise or anti-clockwise?
parts.proper_answer: Draw four concentric circles centred on wire A. Spacing between circles increases with distance from wire. Arrows on all circles in anti-clockwise sense when viewed from above.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the symmetry**
You are looking from above with current coming straight out of the page. There is no special direction left or right, so the field must look the same in all directions around the wire. That gives circles centred on the wire, lying in the plane of the card.

Step 2: **Show weakening with distance**
The magnetic flux density around a straight wire falls off with distance as $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$$ So $B$ is weaker further out. On a field diagram weaker means more widely spaced lines. Draw four circles with gaps getting larger as $r$ increases.

Step 3: **Get the sense with the right-hand grip rule**
Point your right thumb out of the page in the direction of current. Your curled fingers give the field direction. Viewed from above this is anti-clockwise. Add arrowheads on each circle in the anti-clockwise sense.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Explain why a magnetic force is exerted on each wire.

markscheme_points.text: current in (each) wire creates a magnetic field

hints: Hint 1: Start with one wire on its own. What exists in the space around any wire that carries a current?
Hint 2: Now place the second wire in that region. Under what angle condition does a wire carrying current feel a magnetic force $F = BIL \sin\theta$?
parts.proper_answer: Current in each wire produces a magnetic field at the position of the other wire. The current in that other wire is perpendicular (at 90 degrees) to this field, so it experiences a magnetic force $F = BIL$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Each current makes a field**
A current always creates its own magnetic field around it. So wire A creates a magnetic field $B$ at the place where wire B sits, and wire B creates a magnetic field at the place where wire A sits.

Step 2: **Each current sits in the other's field**
A wire carrying current $I$ placed in an external magnetic field $B$ feels a force $$F = BIL\sin\theta$$ Here the wires are parallel and vertical, while the circular field lines are horizontal. So the current is at $90^{\circ}$ to the field, $\sin\theta = 1$, and a maximum force acts on each wire.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: State the directions of the forces.

markscheme_points.text: force on each wire towards other wire

hints: Hint 1: Apply Fleming's left-hand rule on one wire using the circular field direction of the other wire at that point, and think whether the resulting force points inward or outward.
parts.proper_answer: Each force is directed toward the other wire, so the wires attract.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the direction with Fleming's left hand**
Take wire B in the field of wire A. From part (a) the field of A at B points in one horizontal direction. With current up and field sideways, Fleming's left-hand rule gives a force on B toward A. Repeating for A in the field of B gives a force on A toward B. Currents in the same direction attract.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The currents in the two wires are not equal.

Explain whether the magnetic forces on the two wires are equal in magnitude.

markscheme_points.text: Newton's third law pair of forces or force proportional to product of currents

hints: Hint 1: Think about the type of force pair involved when A pushes on B magnetically and B pushes back on A.
parts.proper_answer: Yes, equal in magnitude. The two forces form a Newton's third law action-reaction pair, or $F$ is proportional to $I_A I_B$ so same for both wires.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Equal despite unequal currents**
It is tempting to think the wire with larger current feels a larger force. In fact the force on A is $$F_A = B_B I_A L$$ where $B_B$ is proportional to $I_B$, and the force on B is $$F_B = B_A I_B L$$ where $B_A$ is proportional to $I_A$. Both are proportional to the product $I_A I_B$, so they are equal. This is exactly what Newton's third law requires for mutual interaction forces.
